implementation_notes: rspec-mocks documents method stubs as its core feature: allow(warehouse).to receive(:has_inventory).and_return(false) declares the canned answer on a real object or on a bare double("warehouse", has_inventory: false); and_return accepts several values for consecutive calls, and receive_messages programmes a whole hash of answers in one line. Verifying doubles (instance_double/class_double) add the collaborator's interface to the double, so a renamed method fails instead of silently answering - the Ruby equivalent of Python's autospec - and they are the better default here. A plain object with a method that returns the value remains a good stub where the suite carries no rspec-mocks dependency.
code_sketch:
warehouse = instance_double(Warehouse, has_inventory: false)

order = Order.new("Talisker", 50)
expect(order.fill(warehouse)).to be(false)
# consecutive answers: allow(die).to receive(:roll).and_return(1, 2, 3)
pitfalls: A bare double answers any message (raising only when you ask for verification), so a misspelled collaborator method goes unnoticed; prefer instance_double/class_double.
and_return with several values is consumed in order and the last value repeats, so a test that depends on the sequence breaks when an extra call appears.
allow_any_instance_of and stubbing class methods patch globally for the example and are easy to leak; inject the double instead.

variants.name: Hand-written plain-Ruby stub object
variants.idiom_name: PORO with a method returning the canned value
variants.implementation_notes: Because Ruby resolves messages at runtime, a hand-written object with one method is a complete stub: class StubWarehouse; def has_inventory(_sku, _qty) = false; end and the SUT cannot tell the difference from the real collaborator. This is the zero-dependency route for small collaborators, for library code with no test framework dependency, and for stubs that must also carry a little real behaviour; the trade-off is that Ruby checks nothing for you, so a renamed collaborator method only shows up when the call is made. Where Minitest is the runner, the same object is used directly (or via Minitest::Mock#stub); where RSpec is present, instance_double buys the interface checking that hand-writing does not.
variants.code_sketch:
class StubWarehouse
  def has_inventory(_sku, _qty) = false
end

order = Order.new("Talisker", 50)
raise 'expected out of stock' if order.fill(StubWarehouse.new)
pitfalls: Nothing checks the method signature, so a drifted collaborator contract is discovered only by the runtime error in the test that calls it.
A stub reused across examples keeps whatever state it was given; build it per example or reset it in a before hook.
Implementing only the methods the test calls is fine, but a later code path that calls another method fails with NoMethodError, which is a signal to widen the stub deliberately.
